title: How Storage Really Works
description: Understand the mechanics of storage — from spinning disks to flash memory, page caches, write-ahead logs, and why sequential I/O is king.

segments.text: Storage is the unsung hero of every system. Fast code is worthless if it waits on slow storage. Today we'll see why certain I/O patterns are a thousand times faster than others, and how to exploit that knowledge.

A hard disk drive is a mechanical marvel — spinning platters with a tiny arm sweeping across them, like a record player. To read data, the arm must physically move to the right track and wait for the platter to spin to the right position.

SSDs have no moving parts — they use electrical cells to store data. No seeking, no spinning. Random reads on an SSD are about a hundred times faster than on an HDD. But SSDs still can't match RAM's speed.

Here's the big insight: sequential I/O — reading data in order — is dramatically faster than random I/O on both HDDs and SSDs. For HDDs, the arm doesn't need to jump around. For SSDs, the controller can prefetch and batch efficiently.
This is why databases and log systems are obsessed with sequential writes. An append-only log on an HDD can outperform random writes on an SSD. The access pattern matters more than the hardware.
segments.thought_prompt: Can you think of a data structure that turns random writes into sequential writes?

segments.text: The file system sits between your application and raw disk. It organizes data into files and directories, tracks which disk blocks belong to which file, and handles permissions. Think of it as a librarian managing where every book sits on the shelves.

The OS maintains a page cache — a portion of RAM that caches recently accessed disk pages. When you read a file, the OS checks the cache first. If it's there, you skip the disk entirely. Many database servers 'warm up' because their working set gradually fills the page cache.
Now, here's a scary thought: what if the power goes out while you're writing data? You could end up with half-written, corrupted records. The solution is a Write-Ahead Log — or WAL.

Before changing any data, you first write the intended change to a sequential log file. If the system crashes, you replay the log to recover. It's like a pilot's pre-flight checklist — document what you plan to do before you do it.

PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite — they all use WAL. It's the foundation of crash recovery in virtually every database. And notice: the WAL itself is sequential writes, which we just learned are the fastest kind.
segments.thought_prompt: If WAL guarantees durability, why not just use the log as the entire database?

segments.text: Let's bring it all together: HDDs seek, SSDs don't, but sequential I/O beats random I/O on both. The page cache bridges the RAM-disk speed gap. WAL ensures crash safety through sequential logging. These fundamentals underpin every storage engine you'll ever encounter.
